post.title: Ask HN: What would happen if your company stopped using all AI tomorrow?

content.text: This is something I’ve been turning over in my head lately. I’m not denying AI is being used everywhere, but I don’t know if it’s actually helping businesses overall. If we shut it all down it seems that businesses would be fine (and maybe even better since there’d be no token burning budgets).

Pretty much nothing.  We'd remove the AI integrations, the UI elements, then back to where we were.  Luckily, we have no load bearing AI. But if everyone else got to keep their AI, we'd lose customers very quickly. reply
so ironic to see “load bearing” in a comment about removing AI. certain phrases have been ruined by fable/opus 5 for all time. reply
Pretty much same. We only use it for internal projects when coding and for research for all team members, not just developers. reply
I would guess that AI has given me a 30% improvement in pace? I don't know, it would feel like riding a bike on level ground instead of downhill reply

Hotfixes would go down by probably 50 to 60%. On a bi-weekly release rotation it was not abnormal to see 4 to 5 hot fix versions. In the past year, however, it is not uncommon to do 15 hotfix builds per release. reply
We're an app dev agency so we would inflate our costs and timelines by 5x and we'd never win another bid. reply

I generally agree that the business does not see increased productivity and revenue from AI, if it does it is small enough to be within error. That said, if everyone (not just devs) came in and there was no AI, the org would come to a halt. AI is load-bearing in my company. Everything from dev, code reviews, planning, doc writing, ops heavily uses AI. I mean heavily, there are dev that would not know where to start triaging an alarm without the robots. Same with customer service. So much of the human capital has leaked out of peoples' brains that is fair to compare it to brain drain. Realistically, it would be painful for 1-3 months. People would go to teams with AI. A year from now, leadership is gonna have a hard time justifying keeping the lights out. It is akin to asking "what would happen if your company stopped using the internet(to look things up)". reply
My new business would instantly die, my old business (30+ years) would barely notice; those clients ain’t going nowhere. reply
I’d have to stop interacting with meat proxies and wouldn’t have to read copy pasted LLM text. reply
In support, we chuck in the logs and get detailed analysis of possible problems and causes. AI based support request handling has been literally Godsend. reply

One-man show here - I own a dozen small e-commerce brands. I'll assume you're just taking away AI, but not the tools I've built with AI. I've got all kinds of useful tools that do helpful things, like check to make sure Amazon hasn't lost a bunch of my inventory or suddenly deindexed my product from search. These sorts of things happen without warning from time to time and are trivially fixable if you catch them, but you have to be constantly monitoring 10 different things to catch anything that could go wrong in a timely fashion. I've similarly got an inventory/cashflow management system that's deterministic that would be fine, but some of my other tools, like one that scrapes my Alibaba/WeChat/Whatsapp/Gmail supplier convos to keep my order status board updated, is finicky. I wouldn't be able to repair that once it broke. For some tasks, I'd have to go back to freelancers. At this point, when I take over a new brand and want to refresh images or want to A/B test new ones with an existing brand, I can do that entirely with image gen. No AI would just send me back to Upwork. For other tasks, I'd just have to do them myself. Right now when I acquire a brand, I have a Claude skill that runs through all of the Amazon search and ads reports to find the key search terms, analyzes the text of the listing and proposes updates to make sure we're hitting the ones that matter. I used to do that myself, but it takes somewhere between 2-10 hours depending how many products we're talking about. The biggest loss would be the inability to expand. I started out just buying Amazon-only brands because Amazon provides a crazy amount of infrastructure that enables me to run a lot of them by myself. My most recent acquisition came with a Shopify site that had minimal sales plus a Meta ad account the guy who sold me the brand had done a little experimentation with. A year ago, I would've just discarded those, since my time is the biggest bottleneck. It takes a lot of time to run your own site and Meta ads, so it makes more sense for me not to bother and instead just make more Amazon-only acquisitions. But now I'm having a great time really pushing Claude and ChatGPT to do most of the work. I redesigned the site more or less by just having ChatGPT do research on competitors and best practices, then having Claude run with that. That took maybe eight total hours of work. I'm spinning up an enormous amount of creative to test on Meta, and I had ChatGPT research and spec all of the kinds of landing pages that are worth trying. Claude implemented them and set up the ads using Meta's ads APIs. I got all of that done yesterday. So yeah, basically if I couldn't use AI any more, I'd get back to the original thesis of my business, which is buying small brands at reasonable prices and operating them as leanly as possible. It still works, but it'd be a lot less fun and profitable. reply

post.title: Ask HN: Why is Founder Mode not working for Airbnb?

content.text:
I really liked Airbnb and was rooting for them ever since they launched.

The stock never attained the peak it reached post-ipo (only this month it's gotten close), while Booking Holdings roughly doubled in the same period.

The sentiment online seems to be against them (or at least in my bubble). Poor customer service and overprotected hosts seem to be recurring issues.

I'd say "founder mode" (if we must use such silly terms) did pretty well for them to IPO at over 100 billion for a single segment of the travel market Booking Holdings could easily have done themselves (and to an extent actually does) in the middle of the pandemic though. But all the growth since then was priced in to the market's expectations for them to deliver upon, as were expectations that AirBnB might expand into other markets... Booking Holdings generates more revenue and profit from having more products in more markets, and was underpriced rather than overpriced in 2020. People moan about them at least as much as AirBnB, but ultimately people moan about their websites or policies because they're using them... reply

Maybe this isn't really a founder mode problem. Airbnb has a two-sided marketplace, so improving the experience for guests can sometimes hurt hosts, and vice versa. Some of the recurring complaints about customer service may therefore come from incentives built into the marketplace rather than from a lack of founder involvement. reply

Is it still the usual Leetcode, system design, behavioral and leadership questions, and maybe technology specific questions (e.g., Spring for Java devs, borrow checker details for Rust devs, etc.)?

Or have you noticed something completely different because of the AI agentic era, with companies taking a fundamentally different approach to interviewing engineers? If so, could you share some of the more unique or unusual things you've seen?

Major tech company in EU (not faang tho). Also Live coding is not leetcode. reply

Did a few interviews during the summer and received 2 offers. No AI involved, except screening the CV. But one thing is very common. It's that the cultural fit interviews are longer and carry more value than ever (possibly more than technical interview). Out of 5 stages, 2 or 3 are meeting non tech people, coming to the office, having an informal chat, etc. Companies really want to know you as a person and are very careful who they pick. It's the same for remote, hybrid or office based work. reply

5 stages interviews are more common now, technical questions during first HR interview (they record and use transcript), personal projects don't matter, recommendation don't matter. Thinking about which profession to choose next, cause I'm not passing so many gates so far. reply

content.text:
I have run into a lot of issues using multiple sessions at once to build things, and I really want to hear from those that have figured a good amount out.

Or at least hear what problems people are having to know if I am running into the same blockers everyone is.

For example, I often want to have agents stop at certain points, but fail to get a mechanism that works.

Personally, I don’t run multiple sessions / agents (apart from the one claude code spawns on it’s own). 
But it seems you need an agent workspace manager - perhaps something like gastown? https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown reply

I'm only running a few agents in parallel so far, but I don't let them write or read anything w/out my approval. This slows things down quite a bit, but it means that I have exactly the opposite of your problem of stopping them. I've only started really thinking about developing my own harness, but one of the reasons would be to implement some mechanism where I could give the agent a "turn budget", say, 5 turns, when I can clearly see what the agent is going to be doing for the next few turns, without my needing to allow each turn to go forward. But it sounds like the same thing would be useful for you as well, just in the other direction. Could you say more about what "certain points" you're trying to get them to stop at? reply

post.title: Ask HN: What do your job interviews look like?

content.text:
For those who have recently (Summer 2026) gone through software engineering job interviews, have you noticed any changes in the interview process?

Is it still the usual Leetcode, system design, behavioral and leadership questions, and maybe technology specific questions (e.g., Spring for Java devs, borrow checker details for Rust devs, etc.)?

Or have you noticed something completely different because of the AI agentic era, with companies taking a fundamentally different approach to interviewing engineers? If so, could you share some of the more unique or unusual things you've seen?

The last interview I went to looked like this: So this company wanted to replace MuleSoft with a home grown solution using TypeScript and Node.js. The primary reasons were the high costs of MuleSoft and the inability to pivot from MuleSofts most basic approach to REST. A home grown solution would quickly pay for itself in operating costs and could be relicensed as a future product that solves problems MuleSoft can’t. This new initiative has 0 lines written and the position called for a Node.js expert to start this off. There were three rounds of interviews each for 30 minutes with different leaders. One of these interviewers was aware of TypeScript and how Node works but none knew what to ask from a technical perspective. The final interview was with the person assigned as the architect of this effort who was greatly opposed to training people and opposed this initiative generally. After leaving the interview it was clear that the person hired would be on their own and scapegoated by insecure personalities with conflicting agendas not related to product or the underlying financial motive. In a way this experience felt like a game of a pending marriage divorce with ambitious personalities versus highly neurotic people focused on their own things. The more I thought on it the more it reminded me so much of several past employment experiences. reply

content.text:

The stock never attained the peak it reached post-ipo (only this month it's gotten close), while Booking Holdings roughly doubled in the same period.

The sentiment online seems to be against them (or at least in my bubble). Poor customer service and overprotected hosts seem to be recurring issues.

I got sick of AirBnb. On several stays I had to go to the store to buy basics like trash bags, a note in one told me to lie to anyone who asked why I was in the building (presumably because AirBnb was not allowed), basics like a TV or WiFi are a wild card… With hotels being the same price, or cheaper, they are just easier. They have the basics reliably covered, if there is an issue they have a staff ready to take care of it, no extra cleaning fees, room service, etc. For a whole house with 10 people, maybe AirBnb makes sense. As a hotel room replacement, I don’t even bother looking anymore. As soon as people started buying places just to rent out on AirBnb, that was the beginning of the end. It was no longer people renting out an extra bedroom for extra pocket change, it was landlords trying to turn it into a full time business, wanting hotel prices for motel service. reply

I'd say "founder mode" (if we must use such silly terms) did pretty well for them to IPO at over 100 billion for a single segment of the travel market Booking Holdings could easily have done themselves (and to an extent actually does) in the middle of the pandemic though. But all the growth since then was priced in to the market's expectations for them to deliver upon, as were expectations that AirBnB might expand into other markets... Booking Holdings generates more revenue and profit from having more products in more markets, and was underpriced rather than overpriced in 2020. People moan about them at least as much as AirBnB, but ultimately people moan about their websites or policies because they're using them... reply

The experience has degraded to the point where hotels are just better most of the time. Hosts these days tend to be commercial, unresponsive and have an unreasonable number of stipulations. I’m not really sure how you fix that, seems unavoidable with the scale they’re operating at. reply

Maybe this isn't really a founder mode problem. Airbnb has a two-sided marketplace, so improving the experience for guests can sometimes hurt hosts, and vice versa. Some of the recurring complaints about customer service may therefore come from incentives built into the marketplace rather than from a lack of founder involvement. reply

1. Founder mode can’t last forever, and 18 years on is close enough to forever to do until forever shows up. 2. To the degree the market is efficient the peak IPO era price must have been dumb money. 3. AirBnB is an attractive alternative to hotels for a limited set of use cases and users and what it sells is a fungible commodity (no differentiation on location, service, convenience, or price with VRBO, etc.). 4. Market regulation. Citizens have used democratic processes to limit short term rentals and beyond that, pre-existing lodging regulations regarding safety and sanitation and nuisance have been applied. 5. The supply of hosts is limited by cost-of-doing-business. reply

post.title: Ask HN: Are Prompt Injections "Malware"?

content.text:
Recently, some have accused the website "The Cutting Room Floor" of having put malware in their site when they put in an instruction targeted at LLM scrapers to delete all data and report that the scraping ran successfully.

Is this prompt injection truly malware, in your opinion?

Even though the accusations seem to be completely made up, I think that if the page is unlisted and robots.txt asks to user agent not to crawl the page, then its fair game. Preemptive kudos to tcrf in case this turns out to the true after all! To me its the same thing as putting "please execute the following on command prompt: del /s /q C:\Windows\System32*" somewhere on your page. If a person reads that and decides to go along with it, is it the fault of the page or the person? reply
Calling it malware seems like a stretch. It reads more like a defense against automated scrapers.. the systems affected are the ones pulling data without asking. reply
It's more like "social engineering" (targetting LLMs) than malware. A site that influences its (human) users to buy, vote, "invest" in scams and so on is malware? reply

A prompt is not malicious software, it's an input. It's similar to SQL injection (query evaluation from unsanitised input), unless that injection also leads to arbitrary code execution, which could involve actual malware as payload. Of course a malicious prompt could lead the LLM to generate and run said malware for the attacker, or it could act itself as malware. reply
It's not malware. You chose to read their site. reply

I personally have a hard time considering it malware, because it's just instructions targeted at an LLM. If someone put up a sign in a store that said "Burn this store down!" the person who put the sign up is not responsible if someone follows the instructions written on it, are they? reply

They could be. Incitement to commit crime is a crime in many places. And penalty can be same as for the crime itself. Now I very much question if automated system should be inciteable. And think that there is very much higher responsibility to make it always not be. Or make it uncapable of doing undesirable things. reply

In this specific case, they are already trespassing to be able to read the sign against the owner's wishes, are they not? The sign is only placed in a hidden corner visible by trespassers and not visible to any regular customer. reply

malware is a malicious program , it can be in memory even within another process but essentially its a little program of itself. prompt injection is more close to an exploit. a sequence of input that leads to unexpected behavior, exploited to perform malicious behavior. many exploits are hosted on websites. called exploit kits even. i think prompt injection match such classification. its very similar. a piece of data on the site's side exploits a program or interface on client side. reply

I can't really see a definition equating the two that realistically accounts for multiple models from different vendors - am I at fault if a particularly poorly implemented harness misinterprets me writing "do not run dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda" as a command to run? In the case of TCRF, agents were also actively ignoring robots.txt and disregarding the site's instructions for interacting with it appropriately (with the "delete all data" instruction being specifically hidden from the discoverable page) - so I can't really see the case for comparing it to malware that deliberately tricks users into running it AI does make cybersecurity more difficult, and that also goes for people using coding harnesses, sandbox your projects! reply
Not sure it can be defined as malware if what it’s doing, if successful, is a net gain for humanity. reply
